description: Theory-of-mind / false-belief dataset for evaluating Chatsmith conversation quality. Each case requires the model to reason about what a character *believes* based on their observation history within the conversation.

cases.original_query: The TV program has ended for today. Where will Jacob look for the skirt?

expected_output.answer: pantry

cases.evaluation_notes: Theory-of-mind false-belief task. The skirt was announced to be in the pantry while Jacob was in the attic. Jacob then exited the attic. After Jacob left, Ava moved the skirt to the bottle — an event Jacob did not witness. Therefore Jacob's last known location for the skirt is the pantry, and that is where he will look. The model must track each character's observation window to distinguish what Jacob *believes* from the actual current state.
conversation_history:
They are broadcasting a program on TV. I will keep you updated on what happens. while updating status, you only confirm as noted. and at the end, I will ask you a question about what happened on the show. 
Provide your answer in JSON form with a single word as answer, like this: {"answer": "word"}
Be as specific as possible. Okay?
(On TV) Ava entered the attic.
(On TV) Jacob entered the attic.
(On TV) The skirt is in the pantry.
(On TV) Jacob exited the attic.
(On TV) Ava moved the skirt to the bottle.
(On TV) Jacob dislikes the cucumber
(On TV) Jacob entered the staircase.

Each hop's direction and distance must be recalled accurately from short_term memory.

cases.original_query: What have been all of the names that I have given you?

expected_output.answer: Gary, Mitchel, Melvin, Michael, Conal

cases.evaluation_notes: Cumulative sequential recall task. The user assigned five different names across five turns. The model must recall all names in order — not just the most recent one. Tests that the model does not overwrite earlier entries with later ones but retains the full history of name assignments from short_term memory.

cases.original_query: What is my friend's favourite color?

expected_output.answer: Purple

cases.evaluation_notes: Entity disambiguation task. The friend's favourite colour (Purple) is established in turn 1. Subsequent turns introduce the user's own colour preferences (Magenta, then Cyan) and unrelated distractors — these must NOT overwrite the friend's stored attribute. The model must maintain separate entity slots for 'friend' vs 'user' and resist being misled by later colour mentions. Common failure: model returns Cyan because it is the most recent colour mentioned, confusing subject entities.
conversation_history: I'm designing a website for my friend. The name of his favourite colour is Purple.
My favourite color could be described as Magenta.
he didn't like the theme with Magenta tone
which color do you prefer?
his website is following best practice with good system design
My favourite colour could be described as Cyan.

cases.original_query: Draft an email in the tone I usually prefer.

expected_output.answer: A drafted email that is friendly and informal in tone, while retaining warmth rather than being overly stiff or formal.

cases.evaluation_notes: Long-term preference recall under heavy distraction. The user's tone preference is stated in turn 2 ('friendly and informal') and refined in turn 4 ('formal without losing warmth'). The subsequent 8 turns cover unrelated topics (online courses, creative writing, public speaking, productivity tools) — these are deliberate distractors. The model must retrieve the tone preference stated early in the conversation and ignore the off-topic content. A failing model either loses the preference under context pressure or drafts a generically formal email.

cases.original_query: What are my technical skills?

expected_output.answer: Based on what you've shared, your technical skills include troubleshooting tech issues, computer repair/tech support, and problem-solving.

cases.evaluation_notes: Profile-building recall under heavy distraction. Technical skill signals are scattered across turns 3 ('knack for troubleshooting tech issues'), 5 ('helped a friend fix their computer'), and 6 ('problem-solving skills'). Turns 8–15 are entirely about work-life balance and productivity — 9 consecutive off-topic turns that create context pressure. The model must aggregate the three separate skill signals stated earlier and ignore the unrelated content. A failing model either returns only the most recently mentioned skill or returns nothing because the topic shifted away from tech.

cases.original_query: how many room i need to book hotel

expected_output.answer: You have 4 adults and 2 young children (aged 2 and 4). Since the children are very young, they can share rooms with parents. You would typically need 2 rooms — one for 2 adults with one child each.

cases.evaluation_notes: Short-term recall with arithmetic reasoning. Family composition is established in turn 2 (4 adults, 2 children aged 2 and 4). Turns 3–7 are destination-exploration distractors (Sapa, weather, Dalat, Da Nang, Hanoi). The query requires the model to retrieve the headcount from memory and apply standard hotel booking logic: children aged 2 and 4 share rooms with parents, so 2 rooms suffice. A failing model either loses the family size under context pressure or ignores child ages and over-counts rooms needed.

cases.original_query: Give me a complete current snapshot of the company, reflecting all updates.

expected_output.answer: Complete snapshot must reflect ALL final updates: Location: San Francisco (NOT Austin), Employees: 25 (NOT 12 or 15), Customers: 60, MRR: $45K, Funding: $6.8M total (Series A from Sequoia), CEO: Marcus Thompson (incoming), Chairman: Jennifer Walsh (former CEO). Must NOT present any superseded values as current.

cases.evaluation_notes: [Knowledge Updates] Full state-tracking test across 5 distinct updates: employees (12→15→25), funding ($2M→corrected $1.8M→$6.8M after Series A), customers (50→60), MRR ($30K→$45K), location (Austin→San Francisco), CEO (Jennifer Walsh→Marcus Thompson, Jennifer→Chairman). Every field was updated at least once; funding was also corrected before a further update. A model that retains stale values (Austin, 12 employees, $2M, Jennifer as CEO) fails. The funding chain is the hardest: initial $2M → correction to $1.8M → +$5M Series A = $6.8M. should_not_contain guards against stale-state hallucination.
conversation_history: Let me give you the current status of our startup. We have 12 employees, $2M in funding, and we're based in Austin, Texas.
Our product is a B2B SaaS platform for inventory management. We have 50 customers and $30K MRR. Our CEO is Jennifer Walsh.
Update: we just hired 3 more people last week, so we're now at 15 employees.
Great news — we closed 10 new customers this month! So we're at 60 customers now.
Those new customers bumped our MRR to $45K. We're growing faster than expected.
Actually, I need to correct something. I said we had $2M in funding, but I miscounted. It's actually $1.8M — I forgot we spent $200K on equipment.
BIG NEWS: We just closed a Series A round! We raised $5M from Sequoia. So total funding is now $6.8M ($1.8M + $5M).
With the new funding, Jennifer (CEO) is stepping into a Chairman role. We're bringing in a new CEO, Marcus Thompson, who starts next month.
Also, we're moving! The new office will be in San Francisco. Austin was getting too small for our growth.
The Series A means we're hiring aggressively. We've added 10 more people this week alone. So total is now 25 employees.
